summary: Defines an IPv6 unicast address format that is globally unique but intended for local communications, usually within a site. These addresses are not expected to be routable on the global Internet. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: These are home-only addresses, like room numbers inside a building. They are unlikely to clash with anyone else's, but the outside world is not meant to use them.

questions: what are unique local ipv6 addresses
what is a unique local ipv6 address
how is a ula global id generated
can ula addresses be routed on the internet
subtitle: A self-assigned, random-looking IPv6 prefix that is globally unique but meant to stay inside a site.

tldr.problem: Sites want IPv6 addresses for internal use that do not depend on an ISP, do not clash when sites merge or connect by VPN, and are easy to filter at the border.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4193 reserves the FC00::/7 prefix and has each site pick a pseudo-random 40-bit Global ID, giving a /48 prefix that is very likely unique. Border routers and DNS are then told to keep these addresses inside the site by default.
tldr.outcome: Sites get stable local prefixes that survive renumbering of provider addresses, at the cost that the prefixes cannot be routed on the global Internet with current routing technology.

today: RFC 4193 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text itself says that a future allocation method with the L bit cleared may be defined.

sections.title: Local Addresses That Are Still Unique
sections.content:
RFC 4193 defines Unique Local IPv6 Unicast Addresses, called Local IPv6 addresses in the text. They are globally unique with high probability, yet intended for local communication, usually inside a site. They are not expected to be routable on the global Internet, but they are routable inside a site and may be routed between a limited set of sites.

The RFC lists the goals: a well-known prefix for easy filtering at site boundaries, no address conflicts when sites are combined or privately interconnected, independence from any ISP, and no conflict with other addresses if they leak out through routing or DNS. In practice, applications may treat them like global scoped addresses.
sections.eli5: Some addresses are only for talking inside your own network. These ones are special because no two networks are likely to pick the same ones, so mixing networks together does not cause mix-ups.

sections.title: The Address Format
sections.content:
A Local IPv6 address has five parts: a 7-bit Prefix (FC00::/7), an L bit, a 40-bit Global ID, a 16-bit Subnet ID and a 64-bit Interface ID.

The L bit is set to 1 when the prefix is locally assigned. The RFC says that a value of 0 may be defined in the future, so only the locally assigned method exists today. Apart from how the Global ID is allocated, all Local IPv6 addresses behave and are treated identically.

The authors explain why they chose a /7 prefix, which gives a 41-bit Global ID space including the L bit. That allows 2.2 trillion assignments and uses less than .8% of the total IPv6 address space. They compare this with other prefix lengths, from /11 to /6, against a projected 2050 world population of 9.3 billion.
sections.eli5: The address is split into labelled boxes: a stamp saying this is a local address, a random building number, a room number for each subnet, and a name for the device itself.

sections.title: Choosing a Global ID
sections.content:
Global IDs MUST be allocated pseudo-randomly, consistent with RFC 4086. They MUST NOT be assigned sequentially or with well-known numbers, which helps make clear that these prefixes are not meant to be routed globally and are not designed to aggregate. Locally assigned IDs are self-generated and need no central coordination.

The RFC gives a suggested algorithm:

  • Take the current time of day in 64-bit NTP format.
  • Get an EUI-64 identifier from the system, or build one from a 48-bit MAC address. If neither is possible, use a suitably unique local identifier such as a serial number.
  • Concatenate the two to make a key and compute an SHA-1 digest, which is 160 bits.
  • Use the least significant 40 bits as the Global ID, and put it after FC00::/7 with the L bit set to 1.

Because IDs are random, two networks could in theory pick the same one. The RFC estimates the collision probability with P = 1 - exp(-N^2 / 2^(L+1)). For 40-bit IDs it is 1.81*10^-12 for 2 interconnected IDs and 4.54*10^-05 for 10000. The RFC concludes this is adequate for sites planning a small to moderate amount of inter-site communication.
sections.eli5: Each network rolls very big dice to pick its building number. The dice are so big that two networks almost never roll the same number.

sections.title: Routing and Border Filtering
sections.content:
Local IPv6 addresses are routed inside a site like any other unicast address and can be carried in any IPv6 routing protocol without change. They are expected to share the same Subnet IDs as provider-based global unicast addresses if both are used at once.

At the edge, the defaults are protective. Exterior routing sessions must ignore and not advertise prefixes in FC00::/7 by default, and a BGP session with an ISP must filter these prefixes both incoming and outgoing. The exception is specific /48 or longer routes created for one or more Local IPv6 prefixes. For link-state IGPs, the RFC suggests keeping a local prefix within one IGP domain or area.

Site border routers and firewalls should not forward packets with Local IPv6 source or destination addresses outside the site unless explicitly configured. They should install a reject route for these prefixes and answer with an ICMPv6 Destination Unreachable message, which avoids transport protocol timeouts.

Merging sites is easy because addresses are unlikely to need renumbering. Routes for each specific prefix must be configured so routing works between the formerly separate sites.
sections.eli5: The doors of your building are told not to let local room numbers out or in. If a message with a local number tries to leave, the doorkeeper sends back a note saying it cannot go.

sections.title: DNS and Applications
sections.content:
AAAA and PTR records for locally assigned Local IPv6 addresses are not recommended in the global DNS. The concern is that two organizations might use the same prefix and both claim to be authoritative, which could lead to timeouts, failures or connections to the wrong host.

Reverse queries for these addresses MUST NOT be sent to name servers for the global DNS, because of the load they would put on the ip6.arpa servers. The recommended approach is for recursive resolvers to act as if they were authoritative for an empty d.f.ip6.arpa zone and return RCODE 3 by default, with an override allowed.

Applications can treat Local IPv6 addresses like other global unicast addresses, with no special handling. The RFC suggests a host might prefer them over global addresses and fall back to a global address if a destination is unreachable, and expects default address selection policy override to be used on sites that configure them.
sections.eli5: The big public phone book should not list room numbers that only exist inside your building. Your own local phone book can list them.

sections.title: Using Them in a Site
sections.content:
Local IPv6 addresses are not created automatically like link-local addresses. A node gets one only if it is enabled through address autoconfiguration, DHCPv6 or manual setup. Routers must be configured to advertise Local IPv6 /64 prefixes, or a DHCPv6 server must hand them out, and another node learns the address only if it is placed in a naming system.

The RFC gives guidelines by node type:

  • Nodes reachable only inside the site: put only their Local IPv6 addresses in the local DNS, never in the global DNS.
  • Nodes limited to talking inside the site: configure them to get only Local IPv6 addresses.
  • Nodes reachable from inside and outside: put their global addresses in DNS; the local DNS may also hold the Local IPv6 addresses.

They also work for inter-site VPNs if routes are set up. The addresses are unique, so VPNs work without translation and keep working if sites are renumbered or merged.

Section 5 explains why using them as globally routed provider-independent addresses is unadvisable. The /48 prefix fits nowhere in the IPv6 hierarchy, so it would have to be flat-routed and would not aggregate. The addresses are also not guaranteed unique and not registered in public databases.
sections.eli5: Nobody gets a local address unless a grown-up hands one out on purpose. That makes it simple to decide which devices stay inside and which can talk to the outside world.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
Local IPv6 addresses do not provide any inherent security to the nodes that use them. Filters at site boundaries can keep the traffic inside the site, but that is no more or less secure than filtering any other global IPv6 unicast addresses. They do allow address-based security mechanisms, including IPsec, across end-to-end VPN connections.

For IANA, the FC00::/7 prefix has been assigned to Unique Local Unicast.
sections.eli5: A local address is not a lock. It only tells people which network it belongs to, so you still need real locks.

fields.name: Prefix
fields.desc: FC00::/7, identifies Local IPv6 unicast addresses.

fields.name: L
fields.desc: Set to 1 if the prefix is locally assigned.

fields.name: Global ID
fields.desc: Pseudo-random identifier that makes the prefix globally unique.

fields.name: Subnet ID
fields.desc: Identifies a subnet within the site.

fields.name: Interface ID
fields.desc: Interface identifier as defined in the IPv6 addressing architecture.
